title: Hosea 9:10–17
context: Hosea 9:10–17 begins with the LORD remembering how he found Israel like grapes in the wilderness and early figs, until their fathers went to Baal Peor and became detestable like what they loved (Numbers 25). Ephraim’s glory will fly away like a bird, and the LORD speaks of bereavement and loss of children. In verse 14 Hosea breaks in with a prayer that asks what the LORD will give, and then asks for a miscarrying womb and dry breasts, a grim request often read as asking for a lesser sorrow than seeing children killed. The LORD says all their wickedness is in Gilgal, that he will drive them from his house and love them no more, and that Ephraim’s root has dried up. The unit ends with Hosea saying that his God will reject them because they did not listen, and they will wander among the nations. Shared ground: both traditions read the severe language as covenant judgment spoken with grief, and they read it alongside the LORD’s compassion in 11:8–9.

verses.text: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree at its first season; but they came to Baal Peor, and consecrated themselves to the shameful thing, and became abominable like that which they loved.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he found Israel like grapes in the wilderness and early figs, but at Baal Peor they became detestable like what they loved. Arminians see God’s delight in Israel at the beginning, turned to sorrow by their choice to worship Baal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the principle that people become like what they worship (compare Psalm 115:8). Both traditions note the reference to Numbers 25, and they read the verse as a lament over Israel’s early unfaithfulness.

verses.text: As for Ephraim, their glory will fly away like a bird. There will be no birth, no one with child, and no conception.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Ephraim’s glory will fly away like a bird, with no birth, pregnancy, or conception. Arminian readers see a judgment that reverses the blessing of fruitfulness, which Baal worship falsely promised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God showing that life and fertility come from him alone. Both traditions read the verse soberly, as covenant judgment (compare Deuteronomy 28:18).

verses.text: Though they bring up their children, yet I will bereave them, so that not a man shall be left. Indeed, woe also to them when I depart from them!
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that even if they raise children, he will bereave them, and woe to them when he departs from them. Arminians see the greatest loss as God’s departure, which is worse than any other sorrow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s absence as the heart of judgment. Both traditions read the verse with grief, and they hold the loss of God’s presence as the deepest threat in the passage.

verses.text: I have seen Ephraim, like Tyre, planted in a pleasant place; but Ephraim will bring out his children to the murderer.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he saw Ephraim like Tyre, planted in a pleasant place, but Ephraim will bring out its children to the killer. Arminian readers see a nation once blessed now facing the loss of its children in war.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the contrast between privilege and judgment. Both traditions note that the verse is difficult in Hebrew and translated in different ways, and they read it soberly.

verses.text: Give them—LORD what will you give? Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea prays, asking what the LORD will give, and asks for a miscarrying womb and dry breasts. Arminians see the prophet struggling in prayer, perhaps asking for a lesser sorrow than seeing children killed in war.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the prayer as an expression of anguish. Both traditions read the verse soberly, as the prophet’s grief before God, and they avoid treating it as a pattern for prayer.

verses.text: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal; for there I hated them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds, I will drive them out of my house! I will love them no more. All their princes are rebels.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says all their wickedness is in Gilgal, there he hated them, he will drive them from his house, and he will love them no more. Arminian readers see strong covenant language describing God’s rejection of persistent rebels, while noting that 11:8–9 shows his continuing compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see hated and love no more as covenant terms of rejection rather than emotional spite. Both traditions read the verse alongside 11:8–9, holding judgment and compassion together as Hosea does.

verses.text: Ephraim is struck. Their root has dried up. They will bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, yet I will kill the beloved ones of their womb.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Ephraim is struck, its root dried up, bearing no fruit, and he will kill the beloved ones of their womb. Arminians see a severe picture of judgment, reversing the name Ephraim, which sounds like fruitful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the wordplay on Ephraim’s name. Both traditions read the verse soberly as covenant judgment, without elaborating on its details.

verses.text: My God will cast them away, because they didn’t listen to him; and they will be wanderers among the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says his God will cast them away because they did not listen to him, and they will wander among the nations. Arminian readers see the people’s refusal to listen as the cause of their rejection, so that their judgment is just.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s rejection as a righteous verdict. Both traditions note that wandering among the nations recalls Cain’s fate (Genesis 4:12), and they read the verse as describing exile.
